demographics: Affects all ages and both sexes; young children and older adults have the highest rates of severe illness
More common in warmer months for many bacterial causes
Outbreaks cluster in households, restaurants, catered events and institutions

risk_factors.text: Eating undercooked meat, poultry, eggs or seafood
Eating raw or unwashed produce, or unpasteurized milk or juice
Food left at room temperature more than 2 hours, or poor kitchen hygiene
Recent travel to areas with poor sanitation
Recent restaurant or catered meal, or a known outbreak
Contact with reptiles, amphibians, live poultry or farm animals

social_history: Household members or close contacts with similar GI illness
Attendance at a large gathering or buffet
exposures: Undercooked or raw meat, poultry, eggs, seafood
Raw or unwashed fruits and vegetables, sprouts
Leftover food kept out of refrigeration
Recent restaurant meal or catered event

chief_complaints.text: I've been throwing up and having diarrhea
I feel like I can't keep anything down
I've been running to the bathroom all night

hpi.onset: Sudden, over hours; often within 1–48 hours of the suspect meal, though some organisms cause symptoms days later
hpi.duration: Usually 1–7 days; most resolve without treatment
hpi.progression: Starts with nausea and abdominal discomfort, then vomiting and/or diarrhea; symptoms peak in the first day or two and gradually improve
hpi.location: Diffuse abdominal pain, often periumbilical or lower abdomen
hpi.quality: Crampy, intermittent abdominal pain; watery stools
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate for most; can be severe with profuse diarrhea, vomiting or dehydration
hpi.timing: Cramps come in waves, often worse before a bowel movement

associated_symptoms.text: Lightheadedness or dry mouth from dehydration
Blood or mucus in the stool

pertinent_negatives: Severe localized right lower quadrant pain
Symptoms lasting more than a week
Sick contacts with similar illness before the patient's own symptoms

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants and young children may present with irritability, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers and lethargy rather than clear vomiting or diarrhea; dehydration develops faster.
May have milder fever and less pain but dehydrate quickly; confusion or falls can be the presenting problem.
More severe, prolonged or invasive disease; higher risk of bacteremia and need for hospitalization.
Dehydration and electrolyte loss are tolerated poorly; listeriosis can cause fever, myalgias and fetal loss with few GI symptoms.

general.mild: Alert, comfortable, well hydrated; mild discomfort between cramps
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, frequent trips to the bathroom, dry lips, mild tachycardia
general.severe: Ill-appearing, weak, sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, visibly dehydrated
general.critical: Lethargic or confused, cold clammy skin, minimal urine output, shock

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants, starting away from the area of maximal pain
findings.finding: Diffuse, mild to moderate abdominal tenderness without localization

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the abdomen in all four quadrants
Palpate deeply and ask the patient to cough
findings.finding: No guarding, rigidity or rebound tenderness
No point tenderness at McBurney point

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and tongue
Inspect the eyes and periorbital area
findings.finding: Sunken eyes with reduced tear production

findings.maneuver: Press the fingertip or nail bed and time the return of color
Pinch the skin over the forearm or abdomen and release
Inspect the skin over the trunk and extremities
Assess orientation to person, place and time
Test cranial nerves, strength and sensation
findings.finding: No cranial nerve palsies, weakness, or sensory loss

labs.caveat: Normal or only mildly elevated in most viral and toxin-mediated causes; marked leukocytosis or left shift suggests invasive bacterial infection.
Rises with dehydration and prerenal azotemia; a BUN/creatinine ratio above 20 supports volume depletion.
Rises later than BUN in dehydration; a rising creatinine with oliguria marks acute kidney injury.
Falls with bicarbonate loss in diarrhea; a low bicarbonate with a normal anion gap suggests a non-gap metabolic acidosis.
Hypokalemia from vomiting and diarrhea; can also be high in severe dehydration or acute kidney injury.
Hyponatremia from losses replaced with free water; hypernatremia can occur with poor access to fluids.
Hypoglycemia in children, older adults and poor oral intake.
Elevated with hypoperfusion from severe dehydration or with invasive bacterial infection; guides resuscitation.
A low value favors a viral or toxin-mediated cause; a high value favors invasive bacterial infection.
High specific gravity reflects concentrated urine from dehydration.
From poor intake and vomiting; not specific.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or medication choices; rules out ectopic pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia from dehydration, fever or pain
Sinus rhythm; irregularly irregular rhythm suggests atrial fibrillation from electrolyte disturbance or sepsis
Flattened T waves and prominent U waves from hypokalemia
ST depression or nonspecific ST-T changes with severe hypokalemia or hypoperfusion
Prolonged QT interval from hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia or hypocalcemia

findings.text: Usually normal or shows nonspecific gas and stool patterns; no free air, obstruction or localized ileus
Dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels suggesting obstruction (an alternative diagnosis)

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Severe or localized abdominal pain, suspected surgical abdomen, or when complications such as abscess, perforation or colitis are considered

findings.text: Diffuse small and large bowel wall thickening with mesenteric edema and fluid-filled loops (enterocolitis pattern)
No abscess, free air or vascular occlusion
Colonic wall thickening with pericolic fat stranding suggesting bacterial colitis
Abscess, perforation or toxic megacolon (complicated disease)

imaging.preferred_when: Right upper quadrant pain, jaundice or suspected biliary disease

findings.text: Gallstones or gallbladder wall thickening suggesting cholecystitis (an alternative diagnosis)

initial.why: Assesses dehydration, electrolyte losses and acid-base status; guides fluid and electrolyte replacement
Looks for leukocytosis or left shift suggesting invasive bacterial infection
Rules out pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy before imaging or medication choices
initial.only_if: patient is a person who could be pregnant

initial.why: Identifies bacterial pathogens when antibiotics or public health reporting may be needed
initial.only_if: bloody diarrhea, high fever, severe or prolonged illness, immunocompromise, or outbreak setting

initial.why: Rapidly identifies common bacterial, viral and parasitic causes
initial.only_if: moderate to severe diarrhea, bloody stools, or when a specific pathogen would change management

initial.why: Detects parasites after prolonged diarrhea or travel exposure
initial.only_if: diarrhea lasting more than 7 days, recent travel, or suspected parasitic cause
recent antibiotic use, hospitalization, or healthcare exposure

initial.why: Looks for obstruction or free air when a surgical abdomen is suspected
initial.only_if: severe abdominal pain, distension, or concern for obstruction or perforation

supporting.why: Marks hypoperfusion or invasive infection in severe illness
Supports an inflammatory or invasive process when the diagnosis is unclear
Helps distinguish bacterial from viral causes when antibiotics are being considered
Screens for urinary infection or dehydration
supporting.only_if: dysuria, flank pain, or concern for a urinary source

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.why: Evaluates for complications or alternative surgical diagnoses
supporting.only_if: severe or localized pain, peritoneal signs, or suspected abscess, perforation or colitis
right upper quadrant pain or jaundice

not_indicated.why: Not needed unless pain is epigastric or pancreatitis is suspected
Not indicated unless cardiac ischemia is suspected

decision_points: Assess hydration and vital signs first; oral rehydration is preferred when tolerated, IV fluids for severe dehydration or shock
Stool testing is reserved for bloody diarrhea, high fever, severe or prolonged illness, immunocompromise, recent antibiotics or travel, or outbreak settings
Pregnancy test before imaging or medication choices in anyone who could be pregnant
Avoid antimotility agents when there is bloody diarrhea or high fever because of the risk of worsening invasive infection
Consider surgical consultation for peritoneal signs, toxic megacolon, obstruction or perforation

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease flare
differential.why_considered: Diarrhea, abdominal cramps and fever can mimic an acute infectious gastroenteritis

history: Weeks to months of diarrhea, not hours to days
imaging: Bowel wall thickening with skip lesions on CT or MRI enterography

differential.name: Clostridioides difficile colitis
differential.why_considered: Acute diarrhea with cramping and fever, often after antibiotics
differential.trigger: Recent antibiotic use, hospitalization or healthcare exposure

history: Recent hospitalization or nursing home stay
Watery diarrhea with a distinctive odor
exam: Signs of toxic megacolon in severe cases
labs: Positive C. difficile toxin or PCR
imaging: Colonic wall thickening with thumbprinting on CT

differential.name: Acute appendicitis
differential.why_considered: Nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain can be mistaken for gastroenteritis, especially in children
differential.trigger: Pain migrating to the right lower quadrant with focal tenderness

history: Periumbilical pain migrating to right lower quadrant
exam: Focal right lower quadrant tenderness at McBurney point
imaging: Enlarged non-compressible appendix with periappendiceal fat stranding on ultrasound or CT

differential.name: Ectopic pregnancy
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting in a person who could be pregnant
differential.trigger: Any patient of reproductive age with abdominal pain

history: No diarrheal illness or food exposure
imaging: No intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound

differential.name: Urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis
differential.why_considered: Abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting can accompany a urinary source

differential.name: Mesenteric ischemia
differential.why_considered: Severe abdominal pain with vomiting and diarrhea, especially in older adults
differential.trigger: Pain out of proportion to exam, older patient with vascular risk factors

history: Sudden severe pain, often after meals
exam: Diffuse tenderness with a relatively benign abdomen early
imaging: Vascular occlusion or bowel wall ischemia on CT angiography

differential.name: Scombroid (histamine) fish poisoning
differential.why_considered: Sudden GI symptoms after eating fish, can be confused with infectious foodborne illness

history: Symptoms within minutes to an hour of eating fish
Often multiple people affected at the same meal
labs: No specific lab test; diagnosis is clinical

differential.name: Viral gastroenteritis (norovirus, rotavirus)
differential.why_considered: Overlapping presentation with foodborne illness; often indistinguishable without exposure history

history: Sick contacts with similar illness before the patient's symptoms
labs: Stool PCR may identify norovirus or rotavirus

severity.mild: Acute onset of nausea, vomiting or diarrhea with mild cramps, no fever or low-grade fever, able to tolerate oral fluids, no dehydration, symptoms lasting less than 48 hours
severity.moderate: Persistent vomiting or diarrhea with moderate cramps, low-grade fever, mild dehydration (dry mucous membranes, tachycardia), able to take some oral fluids but may need IV fluids
severity.severe: Profuse diarrhea or vomiting with severe cramps, high fever, marked dehydration (sunken eyes, prolonged capillary refill, reduced skin turgor), orthostatic hypotension, electrolyte abnormalities, unable to tolerate oral intake
severity.critical: Hypovolemic shock, severe electrolyte derangements (hypokalemia, hyponatremia, metabolic acidosis), acute kidney injury, altered mental status, or signs of invasive bacterial infection with sepsis

red_flags.meaning: Suggests invasive bacterial infection (e.g., Shigella, Salmonella, E. coli O157:H7) or inflammatory colitis; requires stool testing and possible antibiotics
Suggests invasive bacterial infection or systemic illness; warrants further workup

red_flags.finding: Severe dehydration (sunken eyes, prolonged capillary refill, reduced skin turgor, oliguria)
red_flags.meaning: Requires immediate IV fluid resuscitation and electrolyte assessment
May indicate hypovolemic shock or sepsis; needs urgent resuscitation
Suggests severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, or sepsis; urgent evaluation
Suggests a non-infectious cause, parasitic infection, or post-infectious complication
Raises concern for C. difficile colitis
Higher risk of severe, prolonged or invasive disease; lower threshold for testing and treatment

complications.name: Electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hyponatremia, metabolic acidosis)
clues: Abnormal bicarbonate and potassium on BMP

complications.name: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)
clues: Bloody diarrhea followed by anemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal failure
Most commonly after E. coli O157:H7 infection

complications.name: Reactive arthritis
clues: Joint pain and swelling weeks after diarrheal illness
May be associated with urethritis and conjunctivitis

complications.name: Guillain-Barré syndrome
clues: Ascending weakness and areflexia weeks after Campylobacter infection

complications.name: Toxic megacolon
clues: Often associated with C. difficile or inflammatory bowel disease

special_populations.differences: Infants and young children dehydrate faster and may present with irritability, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, and lethargy rather than clear vomiting or diarrhea. Oral rehydration is preferred; antiemetics may be used cautiously.
May have milder fever and less pain but dehydrate quickly; confusion or falls can be the presenting problem. Higher risk of severe illness and complications.

Dehydration and electrolyte loss are tolerated poorly; listeriosis can cause fever, myalgias and fetal loss with few GI symptoms. Avoid certain antibiotics (e.g., fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines) and antimotility agents.
More severe, prolonged or invasive disease; higher risk of bacteremia and need for hospitalization. Lower threshold for stool testing, blood cultures, and empiric antibiotics.

key_questions.question: When did the symptoms start, and how long after your last meal did they begin?
key_questions.looking_for: Short incubation (1–6 hours) suggests preformed toxin (Staph aureus, Bacillus cereus); 8–16 hours suggests C. perfringens; 18–72 hours suggests viral or bacterial infection

key_questions.question: What did you eat in the 1–3 days before you got sick?
key_questions.looking_for: Specific high-risk foods: undercooked poultry, eggs, ground beef, unpasteurized dairy, raw seafood, sprouts, leftovers left out

key_questions.question: Have you had diarrhea? Is there blood or mucus in it?
key_questions.looking_for: Bloody diarrhea suggests invasive bacterial infection (Shigella, Salmonella, E. coli O157:H7, Campylobacter) and changes management

key_questions.question: Have you been vomiting? How many times, and can you keep fluids down?
key_questions.looking_for: Profuse vomiting with inability to keep fluids down predicts dehydration and need for IV fluids

key_questions.question: How many stools have you had in the last 24 hours?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequency and volume help gauge severity and dehydration risk

key_questions.question: Any fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: High fever above 102°F suggests invasive bacterial infection; low-grade or absent fever is typical of viral or toxin-mediated illness

key_questions.question: Has anyone else you ate with gotten sick?
key_questions.looking_for: Multiple people ill after the same meal points to a common food source or outbreak

key_questions.question: Have you recently taken antibiotics or been in the hospital?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent antibiotics or healthcare exposure raises concern for C. difficile colitis

key_questions.question: Have you traveled recently, or been around reptiles, amphibians, or farm animals?
key_questions.looking_for: Travel to areas with poor sanitation or animal contact suggests specific pathogens (Salmonella, Campylobacter, parasites)

key_questions.question: Do you have any conditions or take medicines that weaken your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or acid-suppressing medications increase risk of severe or invasive disease

key_questions.question: Are you pregnant, or could you be pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes the differential (listeriosis) and limits medication choices; also rules out ectopic pregnancy and hyperemesis

key_questions.question: How much are you urinating, and are you able to drink fluids?
key_questions.looking_for: Decreased urination, dry mouth, and lightheadedness indicate dehydration

key_questions.question: Any severe or localized abdominal pain, or pain out of proportion to the exam?
key_questions.looking_for: Severe localized pain, peritoneal signs, or pain out of proportion suggests a surgical abdomen or mesenteric ischemia

key_questions.question: Any confusion, weakness, or fainting?
key_questions.looking_for: Altered mental status or syncope suggests severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, or sepsis

reasoning_points: Acute onset of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal cramps after a suspicious meal or food exposure
Incubation period helps narrow the likely organism (toxin-mediated vs. infectious)
Presence or absence of bloody diarrhea, high fever, and severe dehydration guides testing and treatment
Risk factors such as undercooked meat, unpasteurized dairy, travel, animal contact, and immunosuppression are identified
Red flags for invasive bacterial infection, C. difficile, or a surgical abdomen are specifically sought
Pregnancy is excluded before imaging or medication choices
Hydration status is assessed and oral rehydration is preferred when tolerated
Stool testing is reserved for bloody diarrhea, high fever, severe or prolonged illness, immunocompromise, recent antibiotics or travel, or outbreak settings
Antimotility agents are avoided when there is bloody diarrhea or high fever
Alternative diagnoses such as appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, urinary tract infection, mesenteric ischemia, and IBD flare are considered and ruled out

easy: Classic story: sudden nausea, vomiting, and watery diarrhea within hours of a suspect meal
Multiple people ill after the same gathering
Mild dehydration, able to tolerate oral fluids
No blood in stool, no high fever
Clear food exposure (e.g., undercooked chicken, leftover rice)
medium: Bloody diarrhea with fever, requiring stool testing and consideration of antibiotics
Recent antibiotic use raising concern for C. difficile
Older adult or young child with moderate dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities
Symptoms lasting more than a week suggesting parasitic infection
Pregnant patient with fever and myalgias suggesting listeriosis
hard: Immunocompromised patient with severe, prolonged diarrhea and risk of bacteremia
Patient with severe abdominal pain out of proportion to exam suggesting mesenteric ischemia
Overlap with appendicitis or ectopic pregnancy in a patient of reproductive age
Scombroid fish poisoning presenting with flushing and GI symptoms after fish
Patient with no clear food exposure and a non-infectious cause such as IBD flare
